newsitem.title: USA: Clinton refuses to let controversy stop fund-raising.
newsitem.headline: Clinton refuses to let controversy stop fund-raising.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton helped collect more than $1 million for Democratic candidates on Tuesday night, refusing to let a controversy from last year's campaign stop him from fund raising.

With FBI agents investigating fund-raising tactics, Republicans preparing congressional hearings and Clinton himself vowing to change the way campaigns are financed, the president went to the Upper East Side home of Democratic donor Shelby Bryan for a reception for 120 contributors to the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. It raised $1.2 million.
In his remarks, he planned to encourage Democrats not to be scared away from contributing to the party at a time when fund raising has been called into question.

But a rejoinder came in typically New York fashion. Along Clinton's motorcade route was an electronic billboard for Fairway supermarkets that referred to White House coffees in which the guests later made donations to the Democrats. It said:
"Hey, Mr. Clinton! Coffee at Fairway is 65 cents. Coffee at the White House is $200,000. And ours is so much better!!!"
The fund-raiser came less than a month after Clinton announced a voluntary ban on "soft money" contributions over $100,000 to the Democratic National Committee.

Those rules did not apply to the Tuesday night event because it was sponsored by the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which has not adopted the DNC regulations. The fund-raiser had two types of donors: people who gave $10,000 for an individual Senate candidate or $25,000 or more in "soft money" to be spent for general expenses.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said there was a witch-hunt atmosphere in Washington that all fund-raisers were bad and urged reporters to be fair.
"Unless the argument here is that we go to public financing and taxpayers pay for politics, there will be fund-raisers in the future. Candidates will have to raise money," he said.

Republicans, who outspent Democrats by far last year, were busily replenishing their coffers as well. Some 200 Republican big spenders -- members of the party's exclusive "Team 100" -- were golfing, playing tennis and sunbathing with Republican officials and congressional leaders, including House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott, at a posh Palm Beach, Fla., hotel resort this week.

Don Simon, executive vice president of Common Cause, which seeks campaign finance reform, said the Democratic and Republican fund raising was indicative of both sides taking advantage of a "system in a state of total collapse."
"There's kind of an 'anything goes' attitude -- just raise as much as you can from whomever you can in whatever amounts you can get," he said.

McCurry said organisers of the Tuesday night event changed some parts of it "to reflect some of our concerns." The DNC recently adopted guidelines for Clinton's appearances at these types of events to try to prevent a repeat of last year's fund- raising mistakes.

Under the new rules, the name of anyone sitting with Clinton must be submitted 48 hours in advance for checking. No one can sit with the president or have a photograph taken with him who is not a U.S. citizen or if the person represents a foreign-owned corporation.
People attending must submit in advance their titles, occupations, employers and specify whether they are present as an individual or representing a corporation.
Clinton went to the fund-raiser after a day of events spotlighting his efforts to improve the U.S. welfare system. He was to travel on to Boston for an anti-crime speech Wednesday.
